citation: Oil & Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. v. Saw Pipes Ltd. (2003) 5 SCC 705
subject: commercial contract; supply of goods; delay; liquidated damages; penalty; Sections 73 and 74 Indian Contract Act 1872; pre-estimate of loss
holding: Under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, where the parties have agreed to a genuine pre-estimate of damages and actual loss is difficult or impossible to prove, the court or arbitral tribunal is competent to award agreed liquidated damages without proof of actual loss, provided the stipulation is not unreasonable or penal.
headnote: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 — S. 34 — Public policy of India — Patent illegality — Liquidated damages under Ss. 73 & 74 Contract Act.
treatment: Followed and clarified in Kailash Nath Associates v. DDA.

citation: Kailash Nath Associates v. Delhi Development Authority & Anr. (2015) 4 SCC 136
subject: contract breach; commercial agreement; earnest money; forfeiture; liquidated damages; Section 74 Indian Contract Act 1872; proof of actual loss
holding: Under Section 74 of the Contract Act, compensation is payable only upon proof of legal injury or damage actually suffered. Forfeiture of earnest money or deduction of liquidated sums cannot be sustained where no actual loss is proved to have resulted from the breach, especially when the property or goods were subsequently sold without deficit.
headnote: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — S. 74 — Liquidated damages and earnest money forfeiture require proof of actual loss where damage is capable of assessment.
treatment: Landmark authority on Section 74 Contract Act.

citation: Patil Automation Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. v. Rakheja Engineers Pvt. Ltd. (2022) 10 SCC 1
subject: commercial dispute; Section 12A Commercial Courts Act 2015; pre-institution mediation; mandatory prerequisite; rejection of plaint; Order VII Rule 11 CPC
holding: Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, which mandates exhausting pre-institution mediation before instituting a commercial suit (except where urgent interim relief is contemplated), is mandatory. Any commercial suit filed without complying with Section 12A is liable to be rejected at the threshold under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
headnote: Commercial Courts Act, 2015 — S. 12A — Pre-institution mediation is mandatory; non-compliance fatal to commercial suit under Order VII Rule 11 CPC.
treatment: Authoritative constitutional ruling on Section 12A compliance.

citation: Silpi Industries etc. v. Kerala State Road Transport Corporation & Anr. (2021) 18 SCC 790
subject: MSME; delayed payment; Udyam registration; Section 15 16 18 MSMED Act 2006; statutory interest; 3x RBI bank rate; supplier registration date
holding: To claim the statutory benefits of the MSMED Act, 2006 (including statutory 3x RBI compound interest under Section 16 and overriding reference to MSEFC under Section 18), the enterprise must hold an active MSMED/Udyam registration on the date of entering into the contract. Post-contractual registration does not retrospectively apply to prior supplies.
bench: Ashok Bhushan & R. Subhash Reddy, JJ.
headnote: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 — Ss. 15, 16, 17, 18 — Registration mandatory at contract execution date.
treatment: Authoritative ruling on MSME supplier eligibility.

citation: Gujarat State Civil Supplies Corporation Ltd. v. Mahakali Foods Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. (2023) 6 SCC 401
subject: MSME; supplier dues; Section 18 MSMED Act 2006; overriding effect; private arbitration agreement; statutory conciliation; facilitation council MSEFC
holding: Section 18 of the MSMED Act, 2006 contains a non-obstante clause that overrides any bilateral arbitration agreement between the parties. A registered micro or small supplier has an overriding statutory right to approach the MSEFC for conciliation and arbitration, which supersedes private ad-hoc or institutional arbitration clauses.
headnote: MSMED Act, 2006 — S. 18 — Overrides Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and private arbitration clauses by virtue of statutory non-obstante mandate.
treatment: Followed across all commercial courts and arbitral tribunals.

citation: Vidya Drolia & Ors. v. Durga Trading Corporation (2021) 2 SCC 1
subject: arbitration agreement; Section 8 and 11 Arbitration Act 1996; arbitrability of disputes; landlord tenant; tenancy; commercial disputes; non-arbitrable matters
holding: The Supreme Court laid down a comprehensive four-fold test to determine the non-arbitrability of disputes: disputes are non-arbitrable when cause of action arises in rem, affects third-party rights, pertains to sovereign state functions, or is expressly reserved for specialized courts. General tenancy disputes not governed by statutory rent control legislation are fully arbitrable.
bench: N.V. Ramana, Sanjiv Khanna & Krishna Murari, JJ.
headnote: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 — Ss. 8, 11 — Four-fold test for non-arbitrability of disputes.
treatment: Cornerstone precedent on arbitrability in Indian law.

citation: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC & Anr. v. HSCC (India) Ltd. (2020) 20 SCC 760
subject: arbitrator appointment; Section 11 and Section 12(5) Arbitration Act 1996; unilateral appointment; conflict of interest; Seventh Schedule; neutral tribunal
holding: A person who has an interest in the outcome or decision of an arbitral dispute is legally disqualified under Section 12(5) and the Seventh Schedule from acting as an arbitrator, and is equally disqualified from unilaterally appointing a sole arbitrator to adjudicate that dispute.
headnote: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 — S. 12(5) & Seventh Schedule — Ineligibility to unilaterally appoint sole arbitrator.
treatment: Landmark ruling establishing institutional and mutual arbitrator neutrality.

citation: Ssangyong Engineering & Construction Co. Ltd. v. National Highways Authority of India (2019) 15 SCC 131
subject: construction; infrastructure; EPC contract; price escalation; Section 34 Arbitration Act 1996; patent illegality; public policy; award challenge
holding: Clarified the post-2015 amendment scope of Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996: 'patent illegality' must appear on the face of the award and go to the root of the matter. Courts cannot reappreciate evidence or rewrite contractual terms entered into by commercial parties.
headnote: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 — S. 34(2A) — Scope of patent illegality and public policy post-2015 amendments.
treatment: Authoritative standard for Section 34 arbitral review.

citation: Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority (2015) 3 SCC 49
subject: construction contract; building project; engineering delay; arbitral tribunal; evaluation of evidence; Section 34 Arbitration Act 1996
holding: The arbitral tribunal is the ultimate master of the quantity and quality of evidence. An arbitral award based on construction logs, site measurements, and correspondence cannot be lightly set aside unless the finding is so perverse as to shock the judicial conscience.
headnote: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 — S. 34 — Evidentiary primacy of the arbitral tribunal.
treatment: Key precedent for infrastructure and delay claims.

citation: Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors. (2017) 14 SCC 80
subject: commercial contract; force majeure; frustration; Section 56 Indian Contract Act 1872; escalation of costs; economic hardship; supply obligations
holding: Under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, commercial unprofitability, unexpected increase in input prices, or economic difficulty does not constitute frustration of contract. A contract is frustrated only when an unforeseen event wholly destroys the fundamental basis of the contractual obligation.
headnote: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Ss. 32, 56 — Commercial hardship and price escalation do not constitute frustration or force majeure.
treatment: Premier precedent on commercial performance and force majeure.

citation: Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) 8 SCC 746
subject: divorce; matrimonial; mutual consent; Section 13B Hindu Marriage Act 1955; six month cooling off period; waiver; mediation; family settlement
holding: The statutory cooling-off period of six months prescribed under Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 for a second motion in divorce by mutual consent is directory, not mandatory. Where parties have genuinely settled all issues including alimony, maintenance, and child custody through mediation and further cohabitation is impossible, the court can waive the statutory period.
bench: Adarsh Kumar Goel & U.U. Lalit, JJ.
headnote: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 — S. 13B(2) — Six-month cooling-off period for mutual consent divorce is directory and waivable post-mediation.
treatment: Landmark ruling enabling expedited divorce by mutual consent after settlement.

subject: family; matrimonial; maintenance; interim maintenance; Section 125 CrPC; Hindu Marriage Act 1955; Domestic Violence Act; affidavit of assets and liabilities
holding: The Supreme Court framed national uniform guidelines for awarding interim and permanent maintenance across all statutory matrimonial frameworks, mandating the compulsory filing of comprehensive Affidavits of Assets and Liabilities by both spouses to ensure realistic and expeditious determination of financial support.
bench: Indu Malhotra & R. Subhash Reddy, JJ.
headnote: Family Law — Maintenance — Uniform national guidelines and mandatory Affidavit of Disclosure of Assets and Liabilities.
treatment: Binding national code on matrimonial maintenance calculations.

citation: K. Srinivas Rao v. D.A. Deepa (2013) 5 SCC 226
subject: matrimonial dispute; divorce; mediation; pre-litigation mediation; reconciliation; Family Courts Act 1984; mental cruelty
holding: The Supreme Court held that all family courts and trial courts handling matrimonial disputes must actively refer parties to mediation at the earliest opportunity. Even where disputes appear intractable, structured pre-litigation and pendente lite mediation should be pursued to achieve an amicable resolution.
bench: Aftab Alam & Ranjana Prakash Desai, JJ.
headnote: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 — Mediation in matrimonial litigation — Duty of court to explore consensual mediation.
treatment: Pioneering authority mandating mediation in family and matrimonial matters.

citation: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Harsolia Motors & Ors. (2023) 8 SCC 362
subject: consumer; non-commercial civil; Consumer Protection Act 2019; commercial purpose; insurance claim; deficiency in service; indemnity
holding: A transaction is not for a 'commercial purpose' under consumer protection legislation merely because the entity engaged is a commercial enterprise. The purchase of an insurance policy to indemnify against accidental loss does not generate direct profit, and commercial entities remain consumers entitled to redress for service deficiency.
headnote: Consumer Protection Act — Definition of 'Consumer' — Commercial entity taking insurance is entitled to maintain consumer complaint.
treatment: Authoritative ruling on consumer remedies for services.

citation: M/s Meters and Instruments Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. v. Kanchan Mehta (2018) 1 SCC 560
subject: non-commercial civil; personal loan; money debt; cheque bounce; Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act 1881; digital payment; compounding; online settlement
holding: Section 138 proceedings for dishonour of cheques are primarily civil in nature, with the objective of recovering debt rather than penal incarceration. Courts may discharge or compound proceedings even without complainant consent if the accused tenders the full cheque amount with statutory interest and costs via digital transfer.
bench: Adarsh Kumar Goel & U.U. Lalit, JJ.
headnote: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 — S. 138 — Civil recovery character and online compounding through digital payment.
treatment: Leading authority facilitating financial settlement and digital debt recovery.

citation: Afcons Infrastructure Ltd. v. Cherian Varkey Construction Co. (2010) 8 SCC 24
subject: miscellaneous dispute; ADR; Section 89 CPC; mediation; conciliation; judicial settlement; Lok Adalat; civil procedure
holding: Categorized civil disputes into those suitable for ADR (commercial, partnership, consumer, tort, neighbour disputes) and those unsuitable (representative suits, criminal offences, election disputes). Under Section 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure, courts have a positive obligation to refer eligible civil matters to mediation or conciliation.
headnote: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 — S. 89 — Comprehensive taxonomy of disputes suitable and unsuitable for ADR.
treatment: Foundational charter of alternative dispute resolution in India.

citation: In Re: Cognizance for Extension of Limitation (2022) 3 SCC 117
subject: limitation; statutory time limit; Limitation Act 1963; Section 29A Arbitration Act; Section 138 NI Act; commercial court timeframes; limitation extension
holding: The Supreme Court excluded the entire period from 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022 from the computation of limitation for all judicial and quasi-judicial proceedings, including arbitrations under Section 29A and complaints under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, granting a further 90-day grace period.
bench: N.V. Ramana, C.J., Surya Kant & N.V. Ramana, JJ.
headnote: Limitation Act, 1963 — Suo Motu exclusion of COVID-19 period for computing statutory limitation across all Indian proceedings.
treatment: Universal limitation precedent applied across all courts and arbitral tribunals.

citation: Bharat Aluminium Co. (BALCO) v. Kaiser Aluminium Technical Services Inc. (2012) 9 SCC 552
subject: arbitration seat; territoriality; Section 2(1)(e) and 2(2) Arbitration Act 1996; juridical seat; foreign seated arbitration; interim relief
holding: Part I of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 applies only when the juridical seat of arbitration is in India. Where the seat is designated outside India, Indian courts lack jurisdiction under Part I unless expressly made applicable by statutory exception or agreement.
bench: S.H. Kapadia, C.J., D.K. Jain, S.S. Nijjar, Ranjana P. Desai & J.S. Khehar, JJ.
headnote: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 — Ss. 2(1)(e), 2(2) — Seat-centric territoriality principle.
treatment: Constitution Bench judgment establishing the seat-centric regime of Indian arbitration.
